stem: How are assembly language instructions related to machine code instructions?

options.content: Each assembly instruction becomes one machine-code instruction
options.rationale: Correct: the relationship is one to one.

options.content: Each assembly instruction becomes many machine-code instructions
options.rationale: That is true of high-level statements, not assembly.

options.content: Assembly language is itself the binary machine code
options.rationale: Assembly uses text mnemonics that must be translated.

options.content: There is no relationship because they are for different processors
options.rationale: Each assembly language belongs to a processor and maps to its machine code.

explanation: Assembly language is a symbolic form of machine code: one mnemonic per instruction.

stem: What is the job of an assembler?

options.content: To translate assembly language into machine code
options.rationale: Correct: it converts mnemonics and labels into binary.

options.content: To translate a high-level language into assembly language
options.rationale: That is the job of a compiler stage.

options.content: To run machine code one line at a time
options.rationale: Running code is the job of an interpreter or the processor.

options.content: To find syntax errors in a flowchart
options.rationale: An assembler works on assembly text.

explanation: An assembler turns assembly language into machine code.

stem: To which group of instructions does LDD belong?

options.content: Arithmetic
options.rationale: Arithmetic instructions are ADD, SUB, INC and DEC.

options.content: Conditional jump
options.rationale: Conditional jumps are JPE and JPN.

options.content: Input and output
options.rationale: Input and output are IN and OUT.

options.content: Data movement
options.rationale: Correct: it loads the contents of an address into the accumulator.

explanation: LDD, LDM, LDI, LDX, LDR, MOV and STO move data.

stem: What does the symbol table contain?

options.content: Each opcode with its binary value
options.rationale: That is the opcode table of the processor.

options.content: Each label with its address
options.rationale: Correct: it is built in pass 1 and used in pass 2.

options.content: Each variable with the value it is given when the program runs
options.rationale: The table holds addresses, not run-time values.

options.content: Each error found in the program
options.rationale: Errors are reported separately.

explanation: The symbol table maps each label to the address of the line it labels.

stem: In a program, JPE Done appears on line 102 and the label Done is defined on line 120. Why does this need the assembler to make two passes?

options.content: The jump can only be translated by the processor itself
options.rationale: The assembler translates the jump.

options.content: The label Done cannot be used in more than one place
options.rationale: A label can be used many times.

options.content: The address of Done is unknown at line 102
options.rationale: Correct: this is a forward reference.

options.content: The instruction JPE is not in the instruction set
options.rationale: JPE is an instruction of the set.

explanation: A forward reference needs the whole program to be read before every address is known.
hints: When the assembler reads line 102, has it yet reached line 120?

stem: Why is assembly language sometimes used for a small embedded controller?

options.content: It runs without any translation at all by the system
options.rationale: It must be assembled into machine code.

options.content: It gives small, fast programs
options.rationale: Correct: little memory is needed.

options.content: It is portable to every type of processor in use
options.rationale: Assembly is specific to a processor.

options.content: It is easier to read than any high-level language
options.rationale: It is harder to read than a high-level language.

explanation: Direct control and compact code make assembly attractive where memory and power are limited.
hints: Think about memory size and speed.

stem: Why can an assembly language program written for one type of processor not normally be run on another?

options.content: Assembly programs always contain some syntax errors
options.rationale: Syntax errors are not the reason.

options.content: Assembly language has no loops
options.rationale: Assembly programs can loop with jumps.

options.content: The second processor has no memory at all
options.rationale: All processors have memory.

options.content: Each processor has its own instruction set
options.rationale: Correct: the opcodes and registers differ.

explanation: Assembly language is tied to the instruction set of one processor family.
hints: What does each processor family define differently?

stem: During pass 2 an assembler reads the instruction JMP Loop. What does it do?

options.content: Adds Loop to the symbol table of labels
options.rationale: Labels are added to the table in pass 1.

options.content: Runs the jump to test that the program works
options.rationale: An assembler does not run the program.

options.content: Replaces JMP by its opcode and Loop by its address
options.rationale: Correct: both parts are translated.

options.content: Leaves Loop as text for the processor to look up
options.rationale: The processor needs a numeric address.

explanation: Pass 2 converts mnemonics to opcodes and labels to addresses using the completed table.
hints: Which pass builds the table and which uses it?

stem: Machine code is written using text mnemonics such as LDD and STO.
explanation: False. Machine code is binary. Mnemonics such as LDD and STO belong to assembly language.

stem: JPE jumps to a given address if the last comparison found the values equal.
explanation: True. CMP sets a flag; JPE jumps when the flag shows equality and JPN when it does not.

stem: Match each instruction to what it does.

right.content: Load the PC with the address of Start
Compare the accumulator with 0 and set the flag
Load the number 7 into the accumulator
Store the accumulator at the address Total

explanation: Each is an instruction of the 9618 set.

stem: Complete the description of a two-pass assembler.

payload.template: In pass 1 the assembler builds the {{blank:a}} table. In pass 2 it replaces each {{blank:b}} by its opcode and each label by its {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Pass 1: symbol table. Pass 2: opcodes and addresses.

stem:
A program is stored from address 200:

```
200  LDD Num
201  CMP #10
202  JPN Skip
203  LDM #1
204  STO Flag
205  Skip: LDD Flag
206  END
207  Num: 10
208  Flag: 0
```

What address does the assembler put in the symbol table for the label `Skip`?
explanation: Skip labels the line at address 205.
workedSolution:
1. Lines are numbered from 200.
2. The label `Skip:` is on the line numbered 205.
hints: Number the lines from 200 and find the line that carries the label.

stem: Using the program in the previous question, what address is given to the label `Flag` in the symbol table?
explanation: Flag labels the data at address 208.

stem: In pass 2 the address of `Flag` (208) is written as an 8-bit operand in hexadecimal. Write the two hexadecimal digits.
explanation: 208 = 13 × 16 + 0, so the hexadecimal digits are D and 0: D0.
hints: Divide 208 by 16: quotient and remainder give the two hexadecimal digits.

stem: Name the table that the assembler builds in pass 1 to record each label and its address.
explanation: The symbol table records labels and addresses.

stem:
A program is stored from address 300:

```
300  LDM #3
301  STO Count
302  Back: LDD Count
303  DEC ACC
304  STO Count
305  CMP #0
306  JPN Back
307  END
308  Count: 0
```

How many times is the instruction at address 304 (`STO Count`) executed before the program ends?
explanation: Count goes 3, 2, 1, 0, so the store at 304 runs three times.
workedSolution:
1. Count starts at 3 (stored at 301).
2. Pass 1 of the loop: ACC = 2, stored; CMP #0 not equal, jump back.
3. Pass 2: ACC = 1, stored, jump back.
4. Pass 3: ACC = 0, stored; equal, so JPN is not taken.
5. The instruction at 304 runs 3 times.
hints: Trace the loop: Count changes each time round until the comparison is equal.

stem: Describe the two passes made by an assembler. [4]

points.description: Pass 1: each line is given an address
Pass 1: each label and its address is entered in the symbol table
Pass 2: each mnemonic is replaced by its opcode
Pass 2: each label or symbolic address is replaced by the address from the symbol table, producing the machine code

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Pass 1 gives each line an address and records every label with its address in the symbol table. Pass 2 replaces each mnemonic by its opcode and each label by its address from the symbol table to produce the machine code.

explanation: Two marks for each pass.
hints: Which pass does what? Mention the symbol table in both.

stem: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of writing a program in assembly language rather than a high-level language. [3]

points.description: Advantage: the program can be small and fast
Advantage: direct control of the hardware, registers and memory
Disadvantage: harder to write and maintain / not portable to other processors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Advantages: it produces small, fast programs and gives direct control of the hardware. Disadvantage: it is hard to write and maintain and works on one type of processor only.

explanation: Any valid pair of advantages and one disadvantage.
hints: Two advantages and a disadvantage, or the other way round.

stem: Explain what is meant by a forward reference and why it needs more than one pass. [2]

points.description: A forward reference is a use of a label before the line that defines it
The address is not known until the whole program has been read, so a second pass is needed to fill it in

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A forward reference uses a label before it is defined. The address is not known until the whole program has been read, so a second pass is needed.

explanation: Definition and consequence.
hints: When is the address of the label known?

stem:
The program below is to be assembled. It starts at address 400. `IN` puts the ASCII code of a typed character in the accumulator, and `OUT` displays the character whose code is in the accumulator. The ASCII code of A is 65, of N is 78 and of Y is 89.

```
400  IN
401  CMP #65
402  JPE Yes
403  LDM #78
404  JMP Done
405  Yes: LDM #89
406  Done: OUT
407  END
```

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Complete the symbol table produced by pass 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How many instructions refer to a label that is defined on a later line?
parts.explanation: JPE Yes and JMP Done refer forward.
parts.workedSolution:
1. JPE Yes (line 402, Yes at 405) and JMP Done (line 404, Done at 406).
2. Two instructions.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is output if the user types the letter A?
parts.explanation: Equal, so JPE Yes is taken and Y is output.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What is output if the user types the letter B?
parts.explanation: Not equal, so N is loaded and JMP Done skips the Yes line.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe what pass 2 does with the line `JPE Yes`.

points.description: Looks up Yes in the symbol table (405)
Writes 405 as the operand of the machine-code instruction

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It replaces JPE with its opcode, looks up Yes in the symbol table to find 405 and writes 405 as the operand.

explanation: Symbol table: Yes 405, Done 406; 2 forward references; the program outputs Y for A and N for any other key.
hints: CMP #65 compares the accumulator with the ASCII code of A; IN puts the code of the key pressed into the accumulator.

stem: An engineer in Bulawayo writes the control program for a small pump controller in assembly language.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which instruction belongs to the arithmetic group?

options.content: STO
options.rationale: STO moves data.

options.content: JMP
options.rationale: JMP is a jump.

options.content: SUB
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: OUT
options.rationale: OUT is output.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which instruction is a conditional jump?

options.content: JMP
options.rationale: JMP always jumps.

options.content: LDX
options.rationale: LDX loads from an indexed address.

options.content: INC
options.rationale: INC adds 1 to a register.

options.content: JPN
options.rationale: Correct: it jumps only if the comparison was not equal.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State two reasons why the engineer chose assembly language.

points.description: Small program that fits the limited memory
Direct, exact control of the hardware / fast response

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The program is small enough for the limited memory and gives direct, fast control of the hardware.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State two drawbacks of this choice.

points.description: Hard to write, debug and maintain
Not portable: must be rewritten for a different processor

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It is hard to write and maintain, and it has to be rewritten for a different processor.

explanation: Instructions fall into groups; assembly gives control and speed but is processor-specific.
hints: Match each instruction to its group.
